title: Shopping & money
goal: Shop for clothes and other things, ask prices, bargain politely, and point out 'this one / that one'.
intro:
From the old bazaars of Asan and Indra Chowk to roadside stalls in Pokhara, shopping in Nepal often means **bargaining** (मोलमोलाइ). This unit gives you the words for money, prices and clothes, and the demonstratives you need to point things out: यो, त्यो, यी, ती, and their forms before endings (यसको, त्यसमा).

You'll also learn how Nepali says 'I have (money)': **मसँग पैसा छ** 'with me money is'.

vocab.note: Written रु. before the amount: रु. ५००.
भाउ मिलाउनु 'to agree on a price'.
अलि घटाउनुहोस् न 'come down a bit, please'.
कुर्था सुरुवाल: the tunic-and-trousers outfit worn by many Nepali women.
ठिक्क भयो 'it fits perfectly / that's just right'.
यो चाहिँ 'this one (as opposed to others)'.
Also क्यास. Payment apps (QR codes) are very common.
मसँग 'with me': मसँग पैसा छ 'I have money'.

phrases.en: And how much is this one?
Do you have it in another colour?
Do you have one like this, but a bit bigger?

grammar.title: This and that: यो, त्यो, यी, ती
grammar.body:
**यो** 'this' and **त्यो** 'that' (plural **यी** 'these', **ती** 'those') work both as adjectives (यो कमिज 'this shirt') and as pronouns (यो के हो? 'what is this?').

Before an ending like -को, -लाई, -मा, they change to **यस-** and **त्यस-**: **यसको** 'its/of this', **यसलाई** 'to this', **त्यसमा** 'in that'. Plural: **यिनको, तिनको** (or यीहरूको, तीहरूको).

The same y-/ty- pattern runs through the language: यहाँ/त्यहाँ 'here/there', यता/उता 'this way/that way', **यस्तो/त्यस्तो** 'like this/like that', **यति/त्यति** 'this much/that much'.

'This one' in a shop: **यो चाहिँ** (as opposed to the others) or casually **यो वाला**.

examples.en: I want a cap like this.
Not that much — just this much.

grammar.title: 'I have' with सँग, and asking prices
grammar.body:
For things you have on you or own, Nepali says 'with me X is': **मसँग पैसा छ** 'I have money', **मसँग गाडी छैन** 'I don't have a car'. सँग attaches to pronouns and nouns: तपाईंसँग, उहाँसँग, रामसँग. (Relatives use the possessive instead — मेरो भाइ छ — see unit 3.)

**Asking prices**:
• **कति हो?** 'how much is it?'
• **कति पर्छ?** 'how much does it cost?' (lit. how much falls)
• **कतिमा दिनुहुन्छ?** 'for how much will you give it?' — the bargaining question
• **किलोको कति?** 'how much per kilo?' (-को = 'per')

examples.en: I don't have cash right now.
How much are apples per kilo?
How much will you sell this jacket for?
How much for the two altogether?

dialogue.title: Bargaining in Asan
dialogue.setting: Sarah wants to buy a kurtha suruwal at a cloth shop in Asan bazaar, Kathmandu.

lines.speaker: Shopkeeper
lines.en: Come in, didi, what are you looking for?

lines.speaker: Shopkeeper
lines.native: यो हेर्नुहोस्, नयाँ डिजाइन। रातो रङ।
lines.roman: yo hernuhos, nayāṃ ḍijāin. rāto raṅ.
lines.en: Look at this, a new design. In red.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.native: राम्रो छ, तर अर्को रङमा छ?
lines.roman: rāmro chha, tara arko raṅmā chha?
lines.en: It's nice, but do you have it in another colour?

lines.speaker: Shopkeeper
lines.native: छ। यो नीलो छ, यो हरियो।
lines.roman: chha. yo nilo chha, yo hariyo.
lines.en: Yes. Here's a blue one, and a green one.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.en: How much is the green one?

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.native: ओहो, महँगो भयो! अलि घटाउनुहोस् न।
lines.roman: oho, mahaṃgo bhayo! ali ghaṭāunuhos na.
lines.en: Oh, that's expensive! Come down a bit, please.

lines.speaker: Sarah
lines.en: Will you do it for fifteen hundred?

lines.speaker: Shopkeeper
lines.native: हुँदैन दिदी। बोहनी हो — अठार सय लास्ट।
lines.roman: huṃdaina didi. bohani ho — aṭhāra saya lāsṭa.
lines.en: Can't do that, didi. You're my first customer — eighteen hundred, final.

culture: Bargaining is expected in bazaars, at street stalls and with taxi drivers, but not in supermarkets, pharmacies or shops marked **मूल्य निश्चित** (fixed price). Keep it friendly and smiling — a final 'लास्ट?' and a laugh usually works better than walking away. The first sale of the day is called **बोहनी**; shopkeepers believe it sets the day's luck, so they may give a good price — and they may touch the first banknote to their forehead. Nepal's currency is the Nepali rupee (NPR); Indian rupees are widely accepted in the Terai, though large Indian notes may be refused.
